entities.name: Quintus Petilius Secundus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Petilius Secundus, a Roman legionary of Legio XV Primigenia, stands as an unexpected yet potent figure in the study of the Roman Empire, not for any grand achievement, but for the remarkably detailed and well-preserved epitaph discovered in Bonn, Germany. Born around 30 CE, likely in Milan, he served as a common soldier and died at the age of 25 in 43 CE. His tombstone, a rare and intimate glimpse into the life of an ordinary individual, transcends its immediate context to offer profound insights into the social, military, and demographic realities of the Roman frontier during the early Imperial period, making him a crucial, if posthumous, contributor to our understanding of Classical history.

His military career, though brief, reflects the widespread deployment of Roman forces across the burgeoning empire. Secundus was part of Legio XV Primigenia, a legion initially raised by Emperor Caligula in 39 CE and primarily stationed at Vetera (modern Xanten) in Germania Inferior. His epitaph, which details his name, legion, age, and place of origin, suggests a standard progression through the ranks of a Roman soldier, albeit one cut short by an early death. The very existence of such a monument in a frontier province like Germania underscores the Roman practice of commemorating its soldiers, even those far from home, and the establishment of Roman cultural norms in newly conquered territories.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Petilius Secundus, though an ordinary soldier, is historically significant because his well-preserved epitaph offers invaluable primary source data on Roman legionary life, demographics, and funerary customs in the 1st century CE, particularly in the frontier provinces.
